pr_title: [CI] Adding continuous testing for ECS dynamic templates
pr_body:
Closes #96713 

All three tests cases are covered:
- [x] a test document containing all ECS fields with random values in flattened form
- [x] a test document containing all ECS fields with random values in flattened form and index is set with `subobjects: false`
- [x] a test document containing all ECS fields with random values in nested/object form

In addition, I added verification that all ECS multi-field definitions are covered by the ECS dynamic templates (revealing two that actually were not).

@felixbarny @ruflin see if you agree with [my comment](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/97901/files#diff-5de719b6a576263ffb32a9a7a1754078f91b12abf0d4fe7141faeb7a91e6b66dR365-R367) about not failing if we create multi-field mapping even for fields of which ECS definition does not enforce such. 
For example, we define a multi-field mapping for the [`*.name`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/1a254c2f08a54ca4ef4dac6760934f78ebff3b62/x-pack/plugin/core/template-resources/src/main/resources/ecs-dynamic-mappings.json#L115) pattern. If you look into the [ECS definitions](https://github.com/elastic/ecs/blob/main/generated/ecs/ecs_flat.yml), you will find that many `*.name` have multi-field mappings, while many others don't. Trying to be very accurate will result with many more dynamic templates.

@P1llus I assigned you as a reviewer because I think you were waiting for this in order to start migrating some ECS mappings to rely on the builtin dynamic templates.
pr_comments:
> I think that's fine. While on the one hand, this creates a bit more indexing overhead than strictly required, it brings a nice consistency via the naming convention *.name so that users know they can always do a full text search on fields ending with *.name.

I'm not a fan of the ECS multi fields but I agree we should be consistent. Do we have an understand on how much the overhead on storage is? I guess hard to tell? Assuming a user would want to disable this, I assume they could overwrite it in `@custom` and only have the keyword?

> Do we have an understand on how much the overhead on storage is? I guess hard to tell? 

I can't say anything clever about the actual overhead, only that since the default mapping for strings in Elasticsearch is multi-field, then I assume it is at least acceptable. We are only extending ECS a bit here 🙂 

> Assuming a user would want to disable this, I assume they could overwrite it in @custom and only have the keyword?

Exactly! And since we added `logs@custom` [before](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/62bebfd9d6b8dc7f7534ad81c9c7abb0391676be/x-pack/plugin/core/template-resources/src/main/resources/logs-template.json#L8) the ECS dynamic templates, any path or pattern coming from it will take precedence.
@rjernst @mark-vieira would you be able to review or assign someone to review this PR?
I've added a daily ci job with notifications to slack (#es-delivery) and email (logs-plus@elastic.co)

issue_context.title: [CI] Add ECS-mappings compatibility tests
issue_context.body:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/96171 added dynamic templates that cover all ECS mappings.
Those were enhanced by https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/96712 to be applicable with `subobjects: false` as well.

@P1llus wrote a [test](https://github.com/P1llus/testecs) that scans [ECS mapping artifact](https://github.com/elastic/ecs/blob/462b9e5ba80a38d48e5a4a5e14d65726956e512d/usage-example/generated/ecs/ecs_flat.yml#L4), creates a document with all ECS-matching fields, indexes it and verifies that all mappings are as expected.

We want to add this to CI so that it runs on a weekly basis, thus tests regressions in our ECS templates as well as notifying us when ECS gets updated in such a way that requires modification of the dynamic templates.

cc @felixbarny @ruflin
comments:
@mark-vieira this issue is not scheduled yet for implementation, but some guidance would be helpful to have in advance:
- the tests are currently written in Python, is there a simple way to run Python scripts through CI, or should we convert them to Java and run them as JUnit tests?
- @dakrone proposed that we add these tests to a new subdirectory in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/tree/main/x-pack/plugin/stack/qa and have them running as part of the entire test suite both periodically and in PR builds. Can you approve this location and approach?
- there is a single external dependency for these tests- a [generated yaml file from ECS](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elastic/ecs/main/generated/ecs/ecs_flat.yml). Since it is accessible through a static URL, my assumption is that we can simply download it for the test, instead of cloning the ECS repo, can you approve?

> * the tests are currently written in Python, is there a simple way to run Python scripts through CI, or should we convert them to Java and run them as JUnit tests?

If you want to run as part of Elasticsearch CI then reimplementing as JUnit test would be the preferable solution.

> @dakrone proposed that we add these tests to a new subdirectory in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/tree/main/x-pack/plugin/stack/qa and have them running as part of the entire test suite both periodically and in PR builds. Can you approve this location and approach?

That's fine. I also think they could just as well live inside the `stack` project itself rather than create a separate QA project.

> there is a single external dependency for these tests- a [generated yaml file from ECS](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elastic/ecs/main/generated/ecs/ecs_flat.yml). Since it is accessible through a static URL, my assumption is that we can simply download it for the test, instead of cloning the ECS repo, can you approve?

That's probably fine although I wonder if we'll want to version this. Pointing at a file in `main` that's changing makes repeatability difficult. How often do the contents of this file change?

> That's probably fine although I wonder if we'll want to version this. Pointing at a file in main that's changing makes repeatability difficult. How often do the contents of this file change?

These tests are our way to verify that the [ECS dynamic templates](x-pack/plugin/core/src/main/resources/ecs-dynamic-mappings.json) keep up with changes in ECS, so we always want to rely on main and fail if new ECS fields are not covered by these templates. We expect that such failures will be rare and the test would be stable, but if we find out this is not the case we can try something else.

review_comments: Either the assertions or the error logs should contain some hints on how to fix the situation. Something like change ecs-dynamic-mappings.json and add a dynamic template to map field {} to type {}.

@rjernst noted that the problem with fetching from main means that once an ECS change breaks this test, all PRs will fail until we get the dynamic templates (or the test) fixed. @mark-vieira raised a similar [concern](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/96713#issuecomment-1603760192).
I see why relying on main is problematic, but I am not sure what the alternative is. 

If we fetch the `ecs_flat.yml` file from a version branch, for example, it means that we can only capture ECS mismatches after it was already released, which implies that we will ship at least one version with dynamic templates mismatching the ECS of the same version (could be more if we rely on manually updating the used version branch and we fail to do that frequently enough).

I think that a state where `ecs-dynamic-mappings.json` doesn't fully cover ECS should be viewed as a bug. Relying on main provides a good way to ensure that we always release both in sync.

#96713 originally proposed that these tests will run **periodically** but I got advices to add them as yet another test in the suite. Maybe we need to reconsider periodic testing of this?

Any proposals or feedback on that are very welcome.

Summarizing a discussion I had offline with @dakrone: if this test starts failing (due to ECS changes or any other reason), the most straightforward and immediate way to deal with that is to open an issue and annotate it with `@AwaitsFix`. This is one very efficient way to get a quick trigger on such mismatches.

In addition, I made sure to output a very clear indication of what went wrong and how to fix issues related to schema changes. Some such output examples:
1. new ECS field is not covered:
```
[2023-07-31T10:11:25,594][ERROR][o.e.x.s.EcsDynamicTemplatesIT] [testFlattenedFields] ECS field 'client.as.number' is not covered by the current dynamic templates. Update ecs-dynamic-mappings.json so that this field is mapped to type 'long'.
...
ECS is not fully covered by the current ECS dynamic templates, see details above
```

2. wrong type mapping:
```
[2023-07-31T15:21:14,413][ERROR][o.e.x.s.EcsDynamicTemplatesIT] [testFlattenedFields] ECS field 'client.as.number' should be mapped to type 'long' but is mapped to type 'keyword'. Update ecs-dynamic-mappings.json accordingly.
...
At least one field was mapped with a type that mismatches the ECS definitions, see details above
```

3. correct type, but no multi-fields:
```
[2023-07-31T11:23:50,141][ERROR][o.e.x.s.EcsDynamicTemplatesIT] [testFlattenedFields] ECS field 'vulnerability.description' is expected to have a multi-field mapping with subfield 'text'. Fix ecs-dynamic-mappings.json accordingly.
...
ECS is not fully covered by the current ECS dynamic templates' multi-fields definitions, see details above
```

@rjernst @mark-vieira please provide input. We can also decide that we start with relying on ECS main and change if we see it is an issue.

We should have any changes to ECS run these tests so we can avoid this scenario as much as possible. Testing this unilaterally means that any breakages or disruptions are on the Elasticsearch side and that's not ideal. In theory, if every change on either end runs these tests, this scenario should never happen.

Can you assist with setting this up? 
Alternatively, it may be much simpler to run this test daily/weekly. Should be good enough in order to catch inconsistencies soon enough after they are made to ECS main without affecting any other CI run in Elasticsearch.
@mark-vieira how should we proceed with this? Would scheduled daily/weekly builds work?
Where does CI for ECS live currently?

I am not familiar with ECS CI, maybe @ebeahan can assist with that.
This is open for quite some time, what would you say is the best way forward?
Note for reviewer: what would be the right way to download a file from GitHub? For now, I just used `@SuppressForbidden` to be able to test
The better way is probably to declare a custom ivy repo in the build script and have Gradle download it so that' it is cached rather than downloading on every test execution.

Thanks for the proposal! 
Since it is a single file that we download, is adding a dependency on the full repo indeed preferable? What I meant to ask is whether relying on TLS for this single file download good enough.
I am not familiar enough with Ivy- does it require specifying a version of the target repo? If so- this won't address what we need, which is to see ECS changes as soon as they are made. 

If you still think we should replace this, please provide an example that I can use as reference.

You can more or less hard-code the URL in the repo definition. Here's an example we use for [downloading github releases](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/cc2a711b2de2800a34bc34bcc89a4b101485ab37/distribution/docker/build.gradle#L31), but you can adapt it to just download a raw file easily. The placeholders here are for maven artifact ids that look like `[org]:[module]:[revision]`.

I'm not sure if that would translate well to this case, though, as we're downloading a file from main, not from a particular version. Therefore, caching would be difficult, too, unless GitHub supports conditional GETs. But I guess what we could do is to simply download the file in via gradle instead of within the unit test. Something similar to `file("${project.buildDir}/ecs-dynamic-mappings.json") << "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elastic/ecs/main/generated/ecs/ecs_flat.yml".toUrl().text`.

However, that doesn't have many benefits over just downloading the file directly from the unit test itself, except from not having to apply the `@SuppressForbidden` annotation.
We can follow up here. You can set a cache invalidation strategy in the build so it'll redownload but we can attack this at a later time.
So for the time being, are we good with the current approach?
@mark-vieira can I mark this one as resolved? Are you OK with this simple HTTPS file download from GitHub?
Yes, that's fine.
